thread.title: Netflix: Sell-Off Picks Up Steam - Netflix, Inc. (NASDAQ:NFLX)

author: Michael Wiggins De Oliveira
title: Netflix: Sell-Off Picks Up Steam - Netflix, Inc. (NASDAQ:NFLX)
text:
Investment Thesis Netflix ( NFLX ) is a very interesting company. On the one hand, it grew very rapidly, becoming a poster boy for a growth stock. Now that the sell-off in tech is picking up steam, investors will probably be thinking how much lower can Netflix fall? And the answer is, frustratingly, a lot more.
Recent Developments Early last month, I wrote an article titled , Buckle In For Q3 Results . In that article, I address Netflix's capital structure, by focusing in on Netflix's debt. With the benefit of hindsight (which always helps), that turned out to be a great time to exit Netflix's position altogether, as the stock has fallen more than 15% in roughly 5 weeks' time.
However, in this article, I will point out that it is not too late for shareholders to act. One can still exit their investment before Netflix's investment gets really cheap. To explain why Netflix is a bad investment at its present valuation, I'll reverse the case by explaining what Netflix did right.
Netflix's Competitive Advantage: Wall Street Notes Netflix nearly single-handedly changed consumer viewing habits permanently. Not only do consumers have a wider choice of content packages than ever before, but they also have these packages set at an array of pricing points.
And here is the thing. Netflix succeeded phenomenally well in underpricing the competition - and this became their main competitive advantage. Using low prices, allowed consumers to board onto the platform easily, as consumers did not find Netflix cost prohibitive to have a scripted content package. This, in turn, allowed Netflix to grow at a fast clip and reach huge economies of scale.
When Netflix's scale, combined with its huge potential, was attained so quickly, this made others on Wall Street take note.
Imitation Is The Sincerest F orm Of Flattery In the past three years, Disney's ( DIS ) share price has vacillated a whole lot, but at the end of it all, Disney's share price has remained largely unmoved, particularly when compared with Netflix.
DIS data by YCharts So here is the thing. Disney witnessed the positive strides which Netflix was making and resolved to copy Netflix and enter the fray. Towards the end of FY 2019, thus within 12 months, Disney will be offering consumers its own version of its direct-to-consumer platform . Disney is branding its platform, Disney+ .
Disney will be entering this space with a package that will entice consumers with a starting price, which is likely to encroach on Netflix's own competitive advantage .
Furthermore, Disney asserts that its strategy will be revolving more around quality rather than volume, the latter being the avenue adopted by Netflix.
Moving on, other competitors which are also mounting a meaningful challenge to Netflix include Discovery ( DISCK ). Discovery's CEO David Zaslav, for now, has focused Discovery's near-term ambitions on being part of consumers' skinny bundle packages, by joining forces with the likes of DISH ( DISH ), as well as other distributors.
Further down the road, Discovery hopes that its recent hire of Peter Faricy from Amazon ( AMZN ), who helped build its Marketplace, will be successful in exploring Discovery's own opportunities for a direct-to-consumer platform.
Other platforms on offer to consumers include Amazon Video and Apple ( AAPL ) is now launching its own service too. Additionally, Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG ) ( GOOGL ) in investing in its YouTube Premium platform which has started small, but has great potential ahead.
Netflix: The Emperor Has No Clothes And No CFO Back to Netflix. Netflix's growth succeeded in large part due to investors' strong desire for growth opportunities, combined with its exotic-sounding claims around cord-cutting . With many investors truly believing that Netflix had no significant competition.
Nevertheless, even if that had been true - which is not - at the end of the day, Netflix is still a business. And a business is only worth its cash flows discounted back to the present.
For now, as readers know, CFO David Wells has decided to step down from Netflix, with no replacement being named as of yet, which should strike most curious investors with an odd sense of timing.
Although Netflix's CEO Reed Hastings is not a fan of analysts calling Netflix's use of capital a ' cash burn ' preferring instead for calling it to be called an 'investment'. However, I think we should call things how we see them. Netflix is going to burn through $3 billion of free cash flow this year, and next year too. According to Wells, it will be a few years still until Netflix will break-even.
Now, according to CEO Jeff Bezos ,
If you look at large companies, their lifespans tend to be 30-plus years , not a hundred-plus years
Thus, assuming that it will take approximately 4 years for Netflix's free cash flow to break-even, or into 2022, then shareholders paying up $115 billion for Netflix are already pricing in a lot of future growth expectations. Which brings me to the thrust of my argument, Netflix's valuation.
Valuation
Source: Author's calculations, morningstar.com
The above table shows that Netflix is the only company amongst its peers which does not generate any cash flow from operations (or free cash flow for that matter).
Furthermore, for a long time, Netflix was able to boast of its rapidly growing top line, with a CAGR close to 29%.
However, given that Q4 2018's guidance is now pointing to less than that, at 27.8%, investors are starting to weigh up whether the pace of Netflix's growth could start to slow down, as it becomes increasingly more difficult to get the next tens of millions of subscribers onto its platform than the previous tens of millions. Particularly, given the uncompromising competition expected to fight for market share in FY 2019.
Takeaway The article highlights the fact that Netflix faces a critically important junction in its lifespan without a CFO. Additionally, how growth-hungry Disney and Discovery are also exploring how best to launch their own direct-to-consumer platforms - this space is hot. Finally, compounding issues for shareholders is the fact that Netflix is the only company which is both free cash flow negative and a fundamentally overpriced stock.
